title: Given an array containing only three distinct values (for example 0, 1, and 2), sort it in place in a single pass without using a counting approach or a library sort. (LeetCode: Sort Colors)
shortTitle: Dutch National Flag Problem (Three-Way Partition, Sort Colors)

s1_definition.profdef: The Dutch National Flag problem partitions an array of three distinct values into three contiguous groups in a single pass using three pointers: a low boundary for the smallest value, a high boundary for the largest value, and a mid scanner. The scanner swaps smallest values to the low region and largest values to the high region, shrinking the unknown middle until the whole array is partitioned, all in linear time and constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a pile of settlement slips each marked with one of three risk levels: low, medium, or high. He wants them grouped as all low first, then all medium, then all high, and he wants to do it in one sweep. He keeps a boundary on the left for where the next low slip goes, a boundary on the right for where the next high slip goes, and a hand scanning the middle. When his hand finds a low slip he throws it to the left boundary, when it finds a high slip he throws it to the right boundary, and when it finds a medium slip he leaves it and moves on.
s1_definition.oneliner: Three pointers, one pass: send lows to the front, highs to the back, and let mediums settle in the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Dutch National Flag problem partitions an array of three distinct values into three contiguous groups in a single pass using three pointers: a low boundary for the smallest value, a high boundary for the largest value, and a mid scanner. The scanner swaps smallest values to the low region and largest values to the high region, shrinking the unknown middle until the whole array is partitioned, all in linear time and constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a pile of settlement slips each marked with one of three risk levels: low, medium, or high. He wants them grouped as all low first, then all medium, then all high, and he wants to do it in one sweep. He keeps a boundary on the left for where the next low slip goes, a boundary on the right for where the next high slip goes, and a hand scanning the middle. When his hand finds a low slip he throws it to the left boundary, when it finds a high slip he throws it to the right boundary, and when it finds a medium slip he leaves it and moves on.

**One line to remember:** Three pointers, one pass: send lows to the front, highs to the back, and let mediums settle in the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
The simplest approach counts how many of each of the three values exist and then overwrites the array, which takes two passes. The Dutch National Flag algorithm does it in a single pass with three pointers, which is the elegant answer interviewers look for.

We keep `low` starting at 0, `mid` starting at 0, and `high` starting at the last index. The region before `low` holds confirmed smallest values, the region after `high` holds confirmed largest values, and the region from `mid` to `high` is unexamined. We examine `arr[mid]`. If it is the smallest value, we swap it with `arr[low]`, then advance both `low` and `mid`, because the swapped-in element at `mid` is already examined. If it is the largest value, we swap it with `arr[high]` and decrement `high`, but we do not advance `mid`, because the element swapped in from the high end is unexamined. If it is the middle value, we simply advance `mid`.

A finance usage example: suppose risk levels encoded as `[2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]` where 0 is low, 1 is medium, 2 is high. At `mid=0` the value is 2, swap with `high` at index 5, giving `[0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]`, high becomes 4, mid stays. Now `arr[mid]` is 0, swap with `low` at index 0, which is itself, advance both, and so on. The array progressively partitions into lows, then mediums, then highs.

The senior-level nuance: the asymmetry in pointer movement is the crux and the most common source of bugs. When we swap the largest value to the high end, we must not advance `mid`, because we have not yet looked at what came back from the high region, whereas when we swap the smallest value to the low end, the element coming from the low region has already been scanned and is a middle value, so advancing `mid` is safe. The loop continues while `mid` is less than or equal to `high`. This is stable in grouping but not in preserving original order within a group, which is fine for the three-color case.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's risk engine tags each pending settlement with one of three risk levels: low, medium, or high. The operations desk needs the pending queue reordered so all low-risk settlements come first, then medium, then high, so they can clear the safe ones quickly and give extra scrutiny to the high-risk tail. The queue can be very large, so allocating a second array wastes memory, and they want it reordered in one efficient pass.

Problem 2 — A simple counting approach would require two passes over the data, and the desk wants to minimize passes over the large queue, so a single-pass three-pointer partition is preferred.

The code defines a `RiskQueueSorter` class with a `sortByRisk` method implementing the Dutch National Flag algorithm with low, mid, and high pointers. A runnable demo seeds a mixed-risk queue and logs the partitioned result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the risk array `[2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]` where 0 is low, 1 medium, 2 high.

Step 1: The sorter sets low to 0, mid to 0, high to 5. The middle region is the whole array.

Step 2: At mid 0 the value is 2, so it swaps positions 0 and 5, giving `[0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]`, and high becomes 4. Mid stays at 0 because the value brought in from the high end is unexamined.

Step 3: At mid 0 the value is now 0, so it swaps positions 0 with low 0, which is a no-op, and both low and mid advance to 1.

Step 4: At mid 1 the value is 0, swap with low 1, a no-op, both advance to 2. At mid 2 the value is 2, swap positions 2 and high 4, giving `[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]`, high becomes 3, mid stays at 2.

Step 5: At mid 2 the value is now 1, a medium, so mid advances to 3. At mid 3 the value is 1, medium, mid advances to 4. Now mid is greater than high, so the loop ends. The array is fully partitioned as lows, then mediums, then highs.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:25:00 PM com.bank.risk.RiskQueueDemo main
INFO: Before: [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]
INFO: Risk-sorted queue: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
INFO: After:  [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2,0,2,1,1,0]  low=0 mid=0 high=5
    │ mid=2 → swap(0,5) → [0,0,2,1,1,2] high=4 (mid stays)
    │ mid=0 → swap(0,0) low++ mid++ → low=1 mid=1
    │ mid=0 → swap(1,1) low++ mid++ → low=2 mid=2
    │ mid=2 → swap(2,4) → [0,0,1,1,2,2] high=3 (mid stays)
    │ mid=1 → mid++ → mid=3
    │ mid=1 → mid++ → mid=4 > high=3 STOP
    ▼
  [0,0,1,1,2,2]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag problem asks me to sort an array of three distinct values into three contiguous groups in a single pass, and the elegant solution uses three pointers with constant extra space. The naive alternative counts how many of each value exist and then rewrites the array in two passes, which works, but the three-pointer method is the one that demonstrates real command of in-place partitioning.

I keep a low boundary and a mid scanner both starting at the front, and a high boundary at the end. Everything before low is confirmed to be the smallest value, everything after high is confirmed to be the largest, and the region from mid to high is still unexamined. I look at the element under mid: if it is the smallest value I swap it down to the low boundary and advance both low and mid; if it is the largest value I swap it up to the high boundary and decrement high but crucially do not advance mid; and if it is the middle value I just advance mid. I continue while mid is less than or equal to high.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the risk engine. Each pending settlement was tagged low, medium, or high risk, and the operations desk wanted the queue reordered so all the low-risk items came first, then medium, then high, letting them clear the safe ones quickly and scrutinize the risky tail. The queue was large, so a second array was wasteful and extra passes were undesirable, and the single-pass three-pointer partition reorganized it efficiently in place.

The senior-level point I stress is the asymmetry in pointer movement, which is where almost everyone introduces a bug. When I swap the smallest value to the low boundary, the element that comes back to mid from the low region has already been scanned and is a middle value, so it is safe to advance mid. But when I swap the largest value to the high boundary, the element that comes back from the high region has not been examined yet, so I must leave mid where it is and look at the new arrival on the next iteration. Being able to explain exactly why mid advances in one case and not the other is what shows I understand the invariant rather than having memorized the swaps.

---

keyPoints: Comparison sorts: merge sort O(n log n), quick sort O(n log n) average
Non-comparison: counting sort, radix sort — O(n) for limited range
Kth largest: quickselect O(n) average, heap O(n log k)
